newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal rejects EU olive subsidy plan.
newsitem.headline: Portugal rejects EU olive subsidy plan.

text.p: Portugal said on Monday it rejected a European Union plan to reform subsidies for olive farmers because the proposal would destroy production.

Portugal also said that it sought to boost olive production as the industry had strong potential to provide incomes to farmers hit by desertification and to satisfy demand by domestic consumers and export markets.
Now the European Commission offers subsidies based on production rates, but has proposed switching this to a system based on the number of olive trees in order to clamp down on fraud.

Portuguese Agriculture Minister Fernando Gomes da Silva said that under such a proposal farmers receiving subsidies based on the number of trees on their land would have no incentive to produce olives.

"We don't want policy measures that contribute to the destruction of production," he told Reuters on the sidelines of a four-day conference of the International Olive Oil Council (IOC) in Lisbon, which began on Monday.
"The problem is that we need measures that support production and give incentives to develop production," he added.
Earlier, the minister told the conference: "I hope that the IOC sends a statement to the European Union's Agriculture Commissioner opposing a reform based on the number of trees."
More than 50,000 Spaniards protested in Madrid on Saturday against the EU reform proposal.

Spain complains that the new plan would cut vital subsidies to as low as 30 billion pesetas ($207.7 million) from around 100 billion now, crippling an industry that provides thousands of jobs in some of the economically weakest parts of the nation.

Olive oil prices have been falling sharply since last September. Spanish domestic prices had fallen to 370-390 pesetas per kg in early May from just under 600 pesetas last November, the independent Oil World newsletter has said.
Gomes da Silva said he expected the European Commission to take a final decision on whether to implement the reforms by the late summer.

Fausto Luchetti, executive director of the IOC, told Reuters: "If you give an amount (of aid) per tree, regardless what happens with the cultivation of the tree, that surely is a disincentive for olive oil production. That would be the worst system to replace the present one."
He added: "You have to look at the nuances in the measures. But I am confident that the Commission and the present member states will together find a solution."

Luchetti said it was unlikely that the IOC would release a statement responding to the EU reform proposal at the end of the conference, as the matter was for the Commission and member states to resolve.
The IOC represents 24 countries responsible for 93 percent of the world's olive oil production. The EU accounts for about 70 percent of global production.
Gomes da Silva said Portugal would treat the olive oil industry as a priority as it could provide a living to farmers in areas hit by desertification.

"The need to provide incomes to farmers in the most economically depressed and parched areas, the absence of alternative crops and the needs for domestic consumption and to provide exports, make this sector a priority area," he said.
"The prospects of world markets, namely in northern Europe, Asia and America, clearly encourage increased production," he added.
Much of southern Portugal has been hard hit by desertification after a series of droughts, forcing many people from farming families to leave home and seek jobs in the cities.
Gomes da Silva said Portugal would seek to assist the recovery of the olive oil sector.
He said Portugal had about 340,000 hectares of olive trees in 1995, down from some 570,000 in the 1950s.
He added that Portugal now produced an average of about 40,000 tonnes of olive oil annually, down from 120,000 tonnes in the 1950s.
